name: Daria Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior lineworker at the Hollins Cross depot, which is the same depot my dad worked out of for thirty years. I lead a small crew and I take the apprentices out, so a lot of my day is showing a nineteen-year-old how to set a crossarm properly while we change out rotten poles along the farm roads. We do storm calls too, ice mostly, in January and February.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real work, with your hands, and you can see what you've done at the end of the day. I like teaching the young ones the way my dad taught me, at the kitchen table with a coil of rope. What wears me out is the pay, which is low for this region, and head office sending us new forms every month that do nothing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Sam, he's a diesel mechanic at the farm machinery dealer in town. We're getting married next September at St Anne's, where my parents married. So every spare bit of money is going on the wedding, and there isn't much spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get back to work. At church or at the depot, people would say the same, that the computers were never going to climb a pole. I don't really do anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I've never used any of those AI things and I don't want to. If it all blows over, my job stays, the wedding goes ahead, and the apprentices still need someone to teach them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. I'd keep putting money into the wedding, keep training the apprentices, and keep going to the union meetings only when they're about pay. Maybe I'd ask about the senior allowance again in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Has anyone tried to get you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office sent an email about an AI helper for writing up jobs. I deleted it. My handwritten job sheets have never let anyone down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a quiet, normal year look like for you and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wedding in September, then we'd start saving for a deposit on a small house near my parents. Sam wants a garage he can work in. I want a kitchen big enough to have both families over at Christmas.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's get back to work. People at church and at the depot would agree that computers were never going to climb a pole.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I've never used those AI things and don't want to. If it blows over, my job stays, the wedding goes ahead and the apprentices still need teaching.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, putting money into the wedding and training apprentices. Plans to ask again about the senior allowance in the spring.
S0.quote: My handwritten job sheets have never let anyone down.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is rooted in her hometown, her father's depot and her church, and has never used AI. She takes real pride in teaching apprentices. Her thin savings are mostly going into a wedding next September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's nothing wrong with new tools, but don't forget who does the actual work. At the depot I'd say keep the apprenticeships going, because that's how this trade has always worked. You can't learn a pole from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it does worry me. If drones do the patrols and computers do the planning, the depot might need fewer of us, and the apprentices would be the first to go. And I don't want to learn all that new stuff. I'm good at my job as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working, and wait and see what the company actually does. I'd hold off on extras for the wedding, maybe skip the band and have my cousin play instead. If they made training compulsory, I'd do it, but I wouldn't ask for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a cloud over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My apprentice, Kyle. His dad's a farmer and there's not much else for him round here. If the company decides it doesn't need as many apprentices, he's out, and he'd probably end up leaving town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is driving this change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big tech companies in the cities, and people who've never done a day's work outside. They don't think about towns like Hollins Cross. They just think about cutting costs.

S1.say: There's nothing wrong with new tools, but don't forget who does the actual work. Keep the apprenticeships going, because you can't learn a pole from a screen.
S1.think: It does worry me, because if drones and computers take over patrols and planning, the depot needs fewer of us and the apprentices go first. I don't want to learn all that new stuff.
S1.do: Keeps her head down, keeps working and waits to see what the company does. Holds off on wedding extras, such as replacing the band with her cousin, and would only take training if it were compulsory.
S1.feel: Uneasy, as if there's a cloud over everything.
S1.quote: You can't learn a pole from a screen.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line defends apprenticeships and tradition, and privately she admits she doesn't want to learn new tools. She blames big tech and city people who don't think about towns like hers. Her apprentice Kyle is her main concern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when we let big companies run everything. I'd say we need to look after our own, our families and our towns, because nobody else will. I wouldn't be asking for handouts, I'd be asking for proper work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. Two years, the wedding barely done, no savings, no other depot nearby, and I don't know the first thing about computers. Sam's job would probably go too, once the machines fix the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding right down, just family at St Anne's and a meal at my mum's after. I'd keep turning up to work until they tell me otherwise. Sam and I might move in with my parents to save money, and I'd lean on my church and my family, not the government, as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we've had hard times before, and we got through them together. He'd probably offer us the spare room before I asked. He's like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything two years would let you do, or does it feel like too little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Too little. I'm not someone who changes fast, and I'd need years to even think about doing something else. Two years is just long enough to watch it come down the road.

S2.say: This is what happens when we let big companies run everything. We need to look after our own, our families and our towns, and I'd be asking for proper work, not handouts.
S2.think: I'd be scared, with the wedding barely done, no savings, no other depot nearby and no idea about computers. Sam's job would probably go too, once the machines fix the machines.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding down to family at the church and a meal at her mother's house. Keeps working until told otherwise, considers moving in with her parents and leans on church and family rather than government.
S2.quote: Sam's job would probably go too, once the machines fix the machines.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario shakes her deeply, especially with her fiancé's job also exposed. She'd turn to family and church, not the state, which fits her values. She admits she doesn't change fast and two years feels like watching it come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families and communities to get ready, so let's not waste it. I'd say the company should keep apprenticeships going for as long as possible. At church, people would talk about looking after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years helps a bit. The wedding would be done, we'd have time to save, and I could keep working most of that time. But I still don't see myself learning computers, so I'd be hoping for the best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and start saving properly after the wedding, even fifty a week. We'd hold off on the house deposit and stay in our rented place. I'd keep teaching apprentices for as long as the company lets me, because that's what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's there every day, but I can carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't see yourself learning computers. Is there anything that would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my dad told me to, maybe. Or if Sam did it with me. But I'd still feel like I'm giving up something I've spent ten years getting good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, it all falls on us at once. Five, we can at least get married properly and save a bit first. But I'd still be worried about what comes after.

S3.say: Five years is time for families and communities to get ready, so let's not waste it. The company should keep apprenticeships going for as long as possible.
S3.think: Five years helps a bit, because the wedding would be done and we'd have time to save. But I still don't see myself learning computers, so I'd be hoping for the best.
S3.do: Keeps working and starts saving about fifty a week after the wedding. Puts the house deposit on hold and keeps teaching apprentices for as long as the company allows.
S3.feel: Anxious every day, but able to carry on.
S3.quote: I'd still feel like I'm giving up something I've spent ten years getting good at.
S3.fieldNote: Five years mostly helps her protect the wedding and save a little. She still resists learning new tools, though her father or fiancé might persuade her. Her identity is tied up in the skill she's built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people round here are tough. We'll look after each other like we always have. I'd say the young ones should still learn a real trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right for most of it. I'd be thirty-seven and could keep working the poles for a good few years before it really changes. And by then maybe we'd have a little house and something put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep teaching. After the wedding, I'd save steadily and wait to see how things go before changing anything. If the company really needed people to watch over robots, I'd think about it then, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels far enough away to live my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any plans about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I want kids, maybe in three or four years. In this one, I think we'd still go ahead. In the fast one, I'd wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do things the right way. Get married, get a house, have a family, and only then worry. Two years doesn't give me that.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, and people round here are tough, so we'll look after each other like we always have. The young ones should still learn a real trade.
S4.think: I think I'd be all right for most of it, working the poles for a good few years before it really changes. By then maybe we'd have a little house and something put away.
S4.do: Keeps working and teaching apprentices, and saves steadily after the wedding. Waits to see how things go before considering any robot supervision role.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but it feels far enough away to live her life.
S4.quote: Get married, get a house, have a family, and only then worry.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her family plans can go ahead in the right order, which matters a lot to her. She still waits rather than acts. Community and tradition remain her safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right after the wedding, with no savings and both our jobs at risk. What would help is keeping apprenticeships and real jobs going, not handouts, and companies that remember towns like ours exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd lose that isn't money. My dad climbed these poles for thirty years and taught me. If robots do it, who teaches the next girl at the kitchen table with a coil of rope?

headlineQuote: If robots do it, who teaches the next girl at the kitchen table with a coil of rope?
portrait: Daria Farah is a 27-year-old senior lineworker at the same small-town depot where her father worked for thirty years, and she trains the apprentices the way he trained her. She's engaged to Sam, a diesel mechanic, and nearly all her thin savings go towards their church wedding. She has never used AI and doesn't want to, so she's uneasy even in the steady scenario and alarmed by AGI in two years, when she'd lean on family and church rather than government. More time mainly lets her protect the wedding and family plans, while she waits rather than acts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would land right after her wedding, with no savings and both her and her fiancé's jobs at risk.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping apprenticeships and real jobs going rather than handouts, and companies that remember small towns exist.
